relations.notes: Hadad of Baalbek-Heliopolis was worshipped under Rome as Iuppiter Optimus Maximus Heliopolitanus, a documented fusion cult. Preserves supreme weather-sovereignty; the cult image and oracle stay Syrian.

relations.subject: berber_amun_siwa

sources.reference: Corippus, Iohannis (6th c.), naming Gurzil the son of Ammon (the horned/bull god)

relations.notes: Libyan Ammon of Siwa, father of the war-god Gurzil (parentage encoded on Gurzil's record). Expressed as ancestor since 'parent' is not a relation kind.

sources.claim: Ammon was a Libyan (Amazigh) deity whose ram-form oracle stood at the Siwa oasis west of Egypt; Herodotus reckons him a Libyan god, and Greeks identified him with Zeus (Zeus Ammon).

citations.reference: Bates, O. (1914). The Eastern Libyans: An Essay. London: Macmillan & Co., chapter on Religion.

sources.claim: The Siwa oracle of Ammon was one of antiquity's most revered (and the only non-Greek of the seven great oracles); Alexander the Great visited it and was proclaimed son of the god.
Ammon’s Libyan oracle is connected with Egyptian Thebes and Greek Dodona in the foundation accounts reported by Herodotus.

Gurzil was a Berber war-god conceived as the son of Ammon and a cow and depicted as a bull or bull-headed warrior, taken into battle by the Laguatan against the Byzantine general John Troglita (recorded by Corippus, mid-6th c.).

citations.reference: Corippus, Iohannis (De Bellis Libycis), trans. G. W. Shea (1998). Lewiston: Edwin Mellen Press.
Bates, O. (1914). The Eastern Libyans. London: Macmillan, chapter on Religion.

sources.claim: A hilltop sanctuary of Gurzil is plausibly located at Ghirza in Libya, where al-Bakri reports a stone idol still venerated; the cult's priest-chief Ierna was killed defending the image.

citations.reference: Mattingly, D. J. (1995). Tripolitania. London: Batsford.

relations.subject: egyptian_haroeris

sources.reference: Reference treatment distinguishing Haroeris, Horus the Elder, from Horus son of Isis and Osiris.

relations.notes: The registry's Horus is the son of Isis, the heir who contends with Set for the throne. Haroeris belongs to an older layer in which Horus is the sky itself and Set's brother rather than his nephew — the same name covering two genealogies, which Egyptian theology never resolved and this registry does not either.

sources.claim: Haroeris is Horus the Elder, the falcon sky god of the older stratum whose eyes are the sun and moon, brother rather than son of Osiris, worshipped in his own half of the double temple at Kom Ombo.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Haroeris, of the Horus forms and of Kom Ombo.

variants.claim: Whether Haroeris is a separate god or a form of Horus is a matter of convention.
variants.description: Some treatments list Haroeris among the forms of Horus, alongside Harsiese, Harpocrates and Harakhty; others treat him as a distinct older deity whom the Osirian myth later absorbed under a shared name. This registry records him separately because he has his own temple, his own genealogy and his own iconography, and marks the disagreement here rather than deciding it.

sources.reference: Reference treatments of the forms of Horus, which differ on whether Haroeris is a form or a separate deity.

names.value: 'Horus the child'. The Greek rendering keeps the Egyptian phrase almost intact.

relations.subject: egyptian_harpocrates

relations.notes: Horus as an infant — the same god at a different age, and yet worshipped separately, with his own temples, his own amulets and his own Mediterranean-wide following, which is why he is recorded rather than folded in.

sources.claim: Harpocrates is Horus the Child, shown as an infant with a finger to his lips, worshipped widely in the Late Period and across the Greco-Roman world, and invoked on the Horus cippi against venom.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Harpocrates, of the finger-to-lips gesture and of the Horus cippi.

variants.claim: Whether Harpocrates is a separate god or a form of Horus is a matter of convention.
variants.description: He is Horus as an infant, and treatments that enumerate the forms of Horus list him among them. He is recorded separately here because the Late Period and Greco-Roman cult is distinct in practice — its own shrines, its own objects, its own geographic range far beyond Egypt — and because a registry that folded him into Horus would lose all of that. The disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.

sources.reference: Reference treatments of the forms of Horus and of the independent Greco-Roman cult of Harpocrates.

relations.notes: Sirius beside Orion, which is where they are in the sky: Sah rises and Sopdet follows him up.

relations.subject: egyptian_sopdet

relations.notes: Mother of Sopdu, whose name shares her 'sharp' root.

sources.claim: Sopdet is the Egyptian personification of Sirius, whose heliacal rising opened the year and announced the inundation, conflated with Isis and paired with Sah as the parents of Sopdu.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Sopdet, of Sirius and of the Egyptian calendar.

names.value: From a root meaning 'sharp' or 'pointed' — the same word behind Sopdet's name, and behind the word for a pointed thing such as a tooth or a spear.

relations.subject: egyptian_sopdu

sources.reference: Pyramid Texts, which give Sopdu as the son of Sopdet (Sirius) and Sah (Orion).

relations.notes: Son of Sirius and Orion — a celestial family, and the reason his name shares the 'sharp' root with his mother's.

sources.claim: Sopdu is the Egyptian god of the sky and of the eastern frontier, protector of the border outposts and of the Sinai mining expeditions, shown as a crouching falcon or as a plumed Asiatic warrior.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Sopdu, his frontier role, his iconography and his Sinai cult.

names.value: No agreed derivation; the name is known almost entirely from the anti-venom spells that invoke her.

names.value: 'Risen land' or 'exalted earth' — the mound that comes up out of the water, and by extension the Nile silt itself.

sources.claim: Tatenen is the Egyptian god of the primeval mound, the risen land, an androgynous earth god of the Memphis region combined with Ptah as Ptah-Tatenen.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Tatenen, of the primordial mound and of Memphite theology.

names.value: 'Opener of the ways' — wep, to open, and wawet, roads. The name is an office.

relations.subject: egyptian_wepwawet

relations.notes: Not the same god, although almost everyone now reads the upright jackal as Anubis. Wepwawet stands; Anubis lies down. Anubis took over the embalming, the scales and the visual identity, and Wepwawet was reduced to a brother, then to a name people mistake on sight.

sources.claim: Wepwawet, 'Opener of the Ways', is an Egyptian canid god of funerary rites, war and royalty, shown upright on a standard and carried first in processions, with his cult centre at Asyut.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Wepwawet, his standard, his offices and his relation to Anubis.

sources.claim: Werethekau, 'Great of Magic', is the Egyptian goddess personifying the magical power of the royal crowns and the uraeus, shown lion-headed or as a cobra and present at the coronation.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Werethekau, her name, her crown-magic and her royal role.

sources.claim: Aplu (Apulu) is the Etruscan Apollo, son of Tinia and Letun and twin of Artume, worshipped at native sanctuaries including the great temple at Veii; one line of scholarship holds Apulu to be an epithet of the fire god Śuri rather than an independent theonym.

variants.description: One position, reflected in current reference treatment, makes Apulu/Aplu an epithet of Śuri in his character as chthonic sky god. Another treats Aplu straightforwardly as the Etruscan reception of Apollo, with his own major cult at Veii and elsewhere. Both records are kept in this registry and joined by an explicit equated-with edge, because collapsing them would decide a live scholarly question by data-modelling fiat; keeping them unlinked would hide it.

variants.claim: Hercle is kept as a record distinct from Greek Heracles.
variants.description: This registry already keeps `oscan_hercle` separate from `greek_apollod_heracles`, and keeps Tinia, Zeus and Jupiter apart, so the Etruscan Hercle is recorded in his own right rather than folded into the Greek figure. The Greek record carries 'Hercle' among its alternate names as the Italic form of the name; that is noted here so the relation between the entries is legible rather than hidden. The Etruscan figure has his own parentage formula (Tinia and Alchumena), his own apotheosis iconography and his own sanctuaries.

citations.reference: Arrian, Anabasis Alexandri (the most reliable surviving narrative, drawing on the now-lost contemporary accounts of Ptolemy I and Aristobulus); Plutarch, Vita Alexandri; Diodorus Siculus 17 (the only complete contemporary-style narrative that survives, written 1st c. BCE); Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni (1st c. CE); Justin's epitome of Pompeius Trogus 11-12; the Alexander-Romance tradition (Pseudo-Callisthenes c. 3rd c. CE); the Babylonian astronomical diaries (cuneiform contemporary records of Alexander's movements and death-date)

Plut. Alex. 2-3 (the serpent-impregnation narrative); Plut. Alex. 27; Arrian Anab. 3.3-4 (the Siwa Oracle recognition 332 BCE); Diod. 17.49-51; Curt. 4.7.5-32; the Lysimachus posthumous tetradrachms ram-horn iconography

Plut. Alex. 2 — the surface narrative has Philip as biological father with the divine-paternity claim as religious-political overlay; Plut. Alex. 9-10 (Philip openly questioning Alexander's paternity at his second marriage to Cleopatra Eurydice — "Now we shall have legitimate sons"); Just. 9.7

variants.notes: The historical-skeptical reading: Alexander was biological son of Philip II, with the Zeus-Ammon paternity claim functioning as Argead-dynastic religious-political ideology and Olympias's mystery-cult-orientation contribution. Per the registry's standing precedent (Mongán case in Irish tradition: medieval-literary divine-paternity claim about a historical king passes strict-criterion under the literary-tradition reading; same precedent applied to Šulgi at Ur III, Pryderi in Welsh, Bhishma in Hindu), Alexander qualifies under the same criterion. The claim is sustained by contemporaneous oracular recognition (Siwa 332 BCE), by Olympias herself throughout her life, by the Lysimachus posthumous tetradrachms ram-horn iconography, by the continuing Hellenistic Alexander-cult, and by the Alexander-Romance tradition that propagated the divine-paternity claim across the Eurasian textual tradition for two millennia. The dual-paternity reading (Philip biological, Zeus-Ammon divine) is the standard ancient template — already present at Plut. Alex. 2 — and is the same template by which Aegeus + Poseidon become Theseus's dual fathers, Amphitryon + Zeus become Heracles's dual fathers, and Aeson/Tyndareus + the divine partner become standard Greek heroic dual-parentage narratives.

citations.reference: Homer Odyssey 11.260-265, Iliad 24.602-617; Hesiod fr. 181-182; Apollodorus 3.5.5; Euripides Antiope (fragments)

relations.notes: Greeks identified Phoenician Melqart with Heracles from at least the 5th c. BCE. The Cadiz/Gades cult was the syncretic meeting-point — Phoenician colonial foundation that became the principal "Heracles" cult site in the western Mediterranean. Distinct entries retained because Melqart predates the equation by centuries with independent Tyrian-civic identity (the Tyrian biennial egersis ritual, the cypress-wood-only sacrifice taboo, the Herodotean detail that women were excluded from the rite).

relations.notes: Greek Aphrodite ↔ Phoenician Astarte — Herodotus credits the Phoenicians with founding both the Cythera and Paphos cults; the dove iconography, conical stone, and love-and-war dual aspect were inherited from Astarte. The Greek tradition itself acknowledged foreign origin.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_aphrodite

relations.notes: Greeks in Egypt read Hathor of Dendera as Aphrodite. Preserves love, music, and female joy; breaks on Hathor's cow-form, sky-mothering, and her furious Eye-of-Ra aspect, which has no Aphrodisian analogue.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_aphrodite
relations.notes: Hdt: the Arabians call Aphrodite Ourania 'Alilat'. Preserves the heavenly-goddess reading via the Venus-star; breaks on Allat's armed protectress character, which Greeks elsewhere matched to Athena.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_helios

sources.reference: Greek toponym Heliopolis for Iunu (Herodotus, Histories 2.3, 2.59)

relations.notes: Greeks named Ra's city Heliopolis, reading the supreme solar creator as Helios. Preserves the all-seeing solar journey (Ra's barque ~ Helios's chariot); breaks on Ra's creator-kingship, far above Helios's rank.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_helios
relations.notes: Commagene's cult formally fuses Mithra with Helios (later echoed in Roman Mithraism's Sol Invictus Mithras). Preserves all-seeing light; breaks on Mithra's covenant-judging core, absent in Helios.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_hephaestus
relations.notes: Hephaestus ↔ Vulcan per ancient interpretatio. Roman Vulcan was originally a destructive-fire god (the Volcanalia of August 23 was apotropaic — to ward off summer fires from the granaries) rather than a craftsman-god; the metalworking-deity emphasis came with the Greek equation.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_hephaestus

sources.reference: Hdt. 2.99 (the Egyptian Hephaestus = Ptah at Memphis); Plut. De Iside 21

relations.notes: Greek Hephaestus ↔ Egyptian Ptah at Memphis. Ptah is craftsman-creator at Memphis; Hellenistic-era equation produced the syncretic Ptah-Hephaestus cult that persisted at Memphis through the Ptolemaic period.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_hephaestus

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 2.3 (temple of Hephaestus at Memphis)

relations.notes: Hdt consistently calls Ptah of Memphis 'Hephaestus'. Preserves the divine craftsman; breaks on Ptah's creation-by-speech theology (Memphite Theology) — Hephaestus makes things, Ptah thinks the world.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_hephaestus

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos apud Eusebius, Praep. ev. 1.10.11 (Chousor = Hephaistos)

relations.notes: Philo equates Chousor (Kothar-wa-Hasis) with Hephaistos. Preserves the divine smith-architect who arms the gods; breaks on Kothar's magic-and-incantation side and his seat at distant Memphis and Caphtor.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 1.181 (temple of 'Zeus Belos' at Babylon)

relations.notes: Herodotus names Marduk's Esagila/ziggurat precinct 'Zeus Belos'. Preserves kingship over the gods; breaks on Marduk's earned, assembly-conferred sovereignty vs Zeus's inherited succession.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus
relations.notes: Hdt: Persians 'call the whole circle of heaven Zeus'; Commagene fuses Zeus-Oromasdes. Preserves supreme sky-sovereignty; breaks on Mazda's uncreated transcendence and lack of myth-cycle or consort.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos apud Eusebius, Praep. ev. 1.10.7

relations.notes: Philo: 'Beelsamen, in Phoenician lord of heaven, Zeus in Greek.' Preserves the sky-lord title exactly; breaks on Baalshamin's rain-giving weather portfolio, closer to Zeus's storm aspect than his kingship.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: O. Eissfeldt, Baal Zaphon, Zeus Kasios und der Durchzug der Israeliten durchs Meer (1932)

relations.notes: Baal of Mt. Zaphon continued as Zeus Kasios of Mons Casius, a documented cult fusion of Hellenistic date. Preserves the storm-god's mountain seat and seafarers' cult; breaks on Baal's death-and-return cycle.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (2007), ch. 4 on *Dyeus

relations.notes: Name-cognates from PIE *dyeus. Preserves the inherited 'daylight-sky father' etymon; breaks functionally — Luwian Tiwaz developed into a sun-god and oath-keeper, not a storm-wielding king of gods.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: R. Gusmani, Lydisches Wörterbuch (1964), s.v. Lefs/Lews

relations.notes: Lydian Lefs/Lews is the standard scholarly identification of the Lydian Zeus in votive and funerary texts. Preserves the rain-bringer aspect; the Lydian god lacks Zeus's pan-pantheon sovereignty.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: D. Detschew, Die thrakischen Sprachreste (1957), s.v. Zbelsurdos

relations.notes: Roman-era dedications to 'Zeus Zbelsurdos' fuse the Thracian lightning-bearer with Zeus. Preserves the thunderbolt; the Thracian god remains a local mountain-storm power without Olympian court functions.

relations.subject: greek_hesiod_zeus

sources.reference: Epigraphic 'Zeus Sabazios' dedications; cf. Strabo, Geography 10.3.15-18

relations.notes: Imperial-period cult fuses the Thraco-Phrygian horseman sky-father with Zeus as 'Zeus Sabazios'. Preserves the *Dyeus-derived sky-father core; breaks on Sabazios's ecstatic rites and serpent-and-hand cult.

relations.subject: greek_hippolyta
relations.notes: Full sister — both daughters of Ares and Otrera. The variant tradition that has Penthesilea accidentally kill Hippolyta (motivating the Trojan-purification trip) treats them as full sisters by the dominant assignment.

citations.reference: Apollodorus 2.5.9, Epitome 1.16, 5.1; Apollonius Argonautica 2.385-389, 2.966-969; Diodorus 4.16; Plutarch Theseus 26-28; Pausanias 1.41.7, 5.10.9; Hyginus Fabulae 30, 241; Quintus Smyrnaeus Posthomerica 1.18

variants.notes: Variant Athenian tradition: Hippolyta survived the Heracles encounter, was abducted (or befriended) by Theseus on his return-trip from the Amazons, came to Athens, bore Hippolytus to Theseus. Killed in the Amazonomachy battle at Athens when the Amazons came to recover her — by Theseus accidentally or by the Amazon Molpadia per Pausanias.
Late variant: survived to Theseus's wedding to Phaedra; killed herself in grief, or attacked the wedding and was killed.
A few sources have Hippolyta survive the Ninth Labor — surrendering the belt without battle, or surviving the Hera-instigated combat.

names.value: pre-Greek substrate name (the -nthos suffix is non-Indo-European, common in pre-Hellenic toponyms — Corinthos, Olynthos, etc.). The flower-name post-dates the figure; the etiology runs flower-from-Hyacinthus, not the reverse.

relations.subject: greek_hyacinthus

externalRef.name: Zephyrus

relations.notes: The west wind, jealous of Apollo, blew the discus back to kill Hyacinthus per the dominant tradition.

citations.reference: Apollodorus 1.3.3, 3.10.3; Pausanias 3.1.3, 3.10.1, 3.19.3-5; Ovid Metamorphoses 10.162-219; Hyginus Fabulae 271; Athenaeus 4.139d-f; Lucian Dialogi Deorum 16; Philostratus Imagines 1.24

sources.notes: Variant Apollodoran tradition (3.10.3) names Amyclas of Sparta as father — that variant is mortal-mortal and does not produce the demigod classification.

variants.notes: Apollodorus 3.10.3 names Amyclas king of Sparta as Hyacinthus's father (with Diomede as mother — both mortals). Under this variant Hyacinthus would be mortal-mortal and would not pass strict-criterion demigod classification. The registry encodes the Clio-Pierus parentage from Apollodorus 1.3.3 as primary because it is the strict-criterion-demigod-qualifying variant; the Amyclas-Spartan tradition transmitted Hyacinthus's cult-localization at Amyclae but not his demigod status.
Apollodorus has Apollo throw the discus accidentally, without Zephyrus's intervention — pure athletic mishap rather than jealous-wind sabotage.

names.value: Greek: from ὑγιής ("healthy, sound") — "Health" personified. The name is the goddess-personification of physical health; the modern English word "hygiene" derives directly through Latin hygiena from this Greek name.

variants.notes: Variant tradition: the childless Boeotian king Hyrieus hosted Zeus, Poseidon, and Hermes; in gratitude the three gods urinated on a sacrificed bull's hide and instructed Hyrieus to bury it. Ten months later Orion was born from the buried hide. The folk-etymology relates ὥρα/ὁρῶ to οὖρον (urine). Under this variant Orion has three divine "fathers" and no mother — his strict-criterion classification would be deity (3 divine parents averaged); but the Apollodoran Poseidon-Euryale tradition is treated as primary across the registry because the dominant tradition has demigod-tier and the post-mortem catasterism rather than apotheosed-deity.

Apollo, alarmed at Artemis's growing intimacy with Orion, challenged her to hit a distant dark spot in the sea — Orion's head as he swam. She struck before recognizing the target. Discovering what she had done, she placed him in the heavens.

Stung by a giant scorpion sent by Gaia (or by Artemis or Apollo) in punishment for his boast that he could hunt every beast on earth. The scorpion catasterized as Scorpio; the two constellations positioned so that Orion sets as Scorpio rises.

sources.claim: Anshar, 'the entirety of heaven', is the second primordial pair of Enuma Elish with his sister and wife Kishar, son of Lahmu and Lahamu and father of Anu, presiding over the assembly that confronts Tiamat.

variants.claim: Assyrian theology identified Anshar with Ashur.
variants.description: Under the Assyrian empire the national god Ashur was written and understood as Anshar, which promoted him to the head of the Enuma Elish genealogy and let an Assyrian recension put him in Marduk's place. The two are kept as separate records here, with the identification recorded on both: it is a theological move of a particular period, not an original identity.

citations.reference: Oracc AMGG on Ninlil as wife of Enlil and later of Aššur.
Reference treatment of Ashur, his city and the Assyrian recension of Enuma Elish.

variants.claim: Assyrian theology wrote Ashur as Anshar.
variants.description: By reading the national god's name as Anshar, the primordial 'entirety of heaven' of Enuma Elish, Assyrian scholars placed him at the head of the Babylonian genealogy and justified rewriting the epic with him in Marduk's role. The two are kept as separate records with the identification noted on both: it is a theological manoeuvre of a particular empire, not an original identity.

sources.reference: Reference treatment of the Anshar-Ashur identification and the Assyrian recension of Enuma Elish.

names.value: The name has no agreed derivation; the reading Baba is now generally preferred to the older Bau, and both are in use.

relations.subject: mesopotamian_bau

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG s.v. Baba: in sources from Lagash and Girsu her husband is Ningirsu.

relations.notes: Wife of Ningirsu at Lagash. Since Ningirsu and Ninurta are one god by the historical period and Gula is Ninurta's wife at Nippur, this marriage and Gula's are two local faces of the same pairing — which is part of why Bau was drawn into the Gula complex.

sources.claim: Bau, also read Baba, is the daughter of An and wife of Ningirsu, chief goddess of Lagash from the time of Gudea, mother of Igalim, Shulshaga and Ḫegir, with healing associations and the dog as emblem.

citations.reference: Oracc, Ancient Mesopotamian Gods and Goddesses, s.v. Baba.

relations.subject: mesopotamian_enkidu

sources.reference: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I: the gods have Enkidu made as an equal to Gilgamesh, so that Uruk may have peace.

relations.notes: Made deliberately as Gilgamesh's double and counterweight — the epic's premise is that Uruk cannot be governed until the king has an equal. The pair then become inseparable; recorded here as counterpart rather than companion because Gilgamesh's record belongs to the seed core and cannot carry a reciprocal.

relations.notes: Kills the Bull of Heaven with Gilgamesh and then insults Ishtar with its haunch — the second killing, and the one that settles the sentence against him.

sources.claim: Enkidu is the wild man created by the gods as a match for Gilgamesh, civilised by Shamhat, who becomes Gilgamesh's companion, helps kill Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, and dies as the gods' penalty for those killings.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Enkidu: created by the gods as a rival to Gilgamesh, tamed by Shamhat, companion of Gilgamesh, condemned to death after the killings.

relations.notes: His death is the machinery of the Descent: it gives Inanna a reason to be at the gate, and it gives Ereshkigal a mourning that Inanna's arrival interrupts.

relations.notes: Killed by the two of them at Uruk after seven years of famine were promised with him; the killing is the second capital offence charged against Enkidu.

sources.claim: Gugalanna, 'the great bull of heaven', is the husband of Ereshkigal whose funeral rites give Inanna her pretext for descending, and is identified in the epic tradition with the Bull of Heaven killed by Gilgamesh and Enkidu.

citations.reference: Descent of Inanna; Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VI.

variants.claim: Whether the Gugalanna of the Descent is the Bull of Heaven of the epic is debated.
variants.description: Gugalanna is named as Ereshkigal's husband in the Descent and the name means 'great bull of heaven'; the Bull of Heaven of Gilgamesh Tablet VI is the animal Anu gives Ishtar. Many treatments identify the two; others hold that the epic's bull is an instrument rather than the underworld queen's consort, and that the identification is a modern harmonisation. The record states both readings.

sources.reference: Reference treatment noting the long scholarly debate over the dual identity of Gugalanna as celestial consort of Ereshkigal and as the punitive Bull of Heaven of the Epic of Gilgamesh.

names.value: gula means 'the great one'. Ninisina is 'lady of Isin', Ninkarrak and Nintinugga further names of healing goddesses syncretised with her — the aliases here record that syncretism, which was already well advanced in antiquity.

relations.subject: mesopotamian_gula

sources.reference: Oracc, Ancient Mesopotamian Gods and Goddesses, s.v. Gula/Ninkarrak: Gula is the wife of the warrior god Ninurta at Nippur.

relations.notes: Her marriage at Nippur. The pairing is a consequence of the same syncretism that gave her her aliases: as Bau she is the wife of Ningirsu at Lagash, and Ningirsu and Ninurta are one god by the historical period, so the healer of Isin ends up married to the champion of Nippur.

sources.claim: Gula is the Mesopotamian goddess of healing, a divine physician and midwife, syncretised with Ninisina, Ninkarrak and Nintinugga, with cult centres at Isin, Umma and Nippur.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Gula, her role in medicine and her cult centres.

variants.claim: Gula absorbs several originally distinct healing goddesses.
variants.description: Ninisina of Isin, Ninkarrak and Nintinugga were separate goddesses whose cults converged on Gula's; scholarship treats them as distinguishable in origin and largely merged in practice. They are carried here as aliases rather than as separate records, since the merging was already ancient, with this note recording that they began apart.

sources.reference: Reference treatment of the syncretism of Mesopotamian healing goddesses.

names.value: No agreed derivation; the name is written dḪa-ià and may be of non-Sumerian origin.

relations.notes: Husband of Nisaba. The pairing is coherent: she is the goddess of writing and of grain, he is the divine accountant with a grain association, and accountancy for grain is what writing was invented to do.

relations.subject: mesopotamian_haya

relations.notes: Father of Sud of Shuruppak, who is Ninlil under her pre-marriage name — 'Ninlil' is the name Sud receives on marrying Enlil. This registry keeps one record, Ninlil, with Sud noted there, so the paternity is recorded as a link to that record.

sources.claim: Haya is the Mesopotamian god of scribes, a divine accountant, archivist and doorkeeper with a grain association, husband of Nisaba and father of Sud, worshipped chiefly in the Ur III period.

citations.reference: Oracc, Ancient Mesopotamian Gods and Goddesses, s.v. Haya.

Sumerian King List entry for Gilgamesh: "Gilgamesh, his father was a phantom (lillu), the en/lord of Kulaba"

variants.notes: The Sumerian King List records Gilgamesh's father not as Lugalbanda but as a "divine phantom (lillu) lord of Kulaba." Some scholars (per Nature genetics article cited above) read this as a dual-paternity tradition — Lugalbanda as legal/social father, the divine lillu-phantom as biological — analogous to Aethra-Aegeus-Poseidon. Other scholars treat it as a separate tradition incompatible with the Lugalbanda-paternity reading. Under the dual-paternity reading, Gilgamesh would have two divine and one mortal parent (the phantom-lord + Ninsun + Lugalbanda) — the source of the "two-thirds god, one-third mortal" arithmetic.

sources.reference: DDD (2nd ed. 1999), s.v. 'Astarte'; M. S. Smith, The Early History of God (2002)

relations.notes: Reciprocal of canaanite_athtart.equated-with — Ugaritic ʿAṯtartu and Phoenician ʿAštart are the same goddess in Bronze and Iron Age streams. Preserves war, love, and the Venus-star; the Iron Age Phoenician goddess gains far greater cultic prominence.

relations.subject: phoenician_astarte

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos apud Eusebius, Praep. ev. 1.10.32

relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_hesiod_aphrodite.interpretatio — Philo: 'Astarte the Phoenicians say is Aphrodite'; Hdt derives Ourania's cult from Phoenicia. Preserves love + evening-star; breaks on Astarte's war portfolio, which Greek Aphrodite largely shed.

relations.subject: phoenician_astarte
relations.notes: ʿAštart and Ištar descend from common Semitic *ʿAṯtar-, sharing the love-war-Venus complex. Cognate development, not borrowing: each goddess's cult, consorts, and myths evolved independently.

relations.subject: phoenician_astarte
relations.notes: The Pyrgi bilingual dedicates one sanctuary 'to Astarte' (Phoenician) = 'to Uni' (Etruscan) — a state-level ancient equation. Preserves supreme-goddess rank; Uni's Hera-like matronage fits Astarte poorly.

sources.reference: Hdt. 1.105 ("the most ancient temple of Aphrodite was founded from the Phoenician Ascalon shrine"); Paus. 1.14.7; Tac. Hist. 2.3 (the conical Paphian stone)
Plut. De Iside 15-16 (the Byblos Astarte who hosted Isis on her quest for Osiris's body)

citations.reference: Sidonian royal sarcophagi (Tabnit, Eshmunazar II); Byblos inscriptions

relations.subject: phoenician_baal_hammon

relations.subject: phoenician_baal_hammon
relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_hesiod_cronus.interpretatio — Greek writers call Carthage's supreme god Kronos, via the Tophet child-offering motif matched to Kronos devouring children. Preserves the aged-supreme-father slot; the equation is driven by Greek polemic.

relations.subject: phoenician_baal_hammon
relations.notes: Under Rome, Baal Hammon's African cult continued wholesale as Saturnus — the dominant god of Roman Africa. Preserves the aged supreme father and the vow-offering (molk) system; the Roman name is a shell.

citations.reference: Punic dedicatory inscriptions, Tophet of Salammbô, Carthage
Philo of Byblos via Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica (Kronos)

names.value: 'Lady of Byblos' — baʿalat is the feminine of baʿal, 'lord', and Gebal is the Semitic name of the city the Greeks called Byblos.

relations.subject: phoenician_baalat_gebal

sources.reference: Reference treatment of Baalat Gebal, equated with the Egyptian goddess Hathor by the 12th dynasty and represented in Egyptian dress.

relations.notes: Equated with Hathor, and drawn as her: Byblos sold cedar and papyrus to Egypt for two thousand years and its goddess is dressed accordingly.

sources.claim: Baalat Gebal, 'Lady of Byblos', is the chief deity of Byblos, a goddess of earth and fertility and protector of its kings, equated with the Egyptian Hathor and represented in Egyptian dress.

citations.reference: Reference treatments of Baalat Gebal, her temple and her equation with Hathor.

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos, quoted in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 1.10.7
Philo of Byblos, quoted in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 1.10.7

relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_hesiod_zeus.interpretatio — Philo: 'Beelsamen, in Phoenician lord of heaven, Zeus in Greek.' Preserves the sky-lord title exactly; breaks on Baalshamin's rain-giving weather portfolio, closer to Zeus's storm aspect than his kingship.

relations.subject: phoenician_baalshamin

relations.notes: Reciprocal of luwian_tarhunz.interpretatio — The Karatepe bilingual translates Tarhunzas of Heaven as Baal Shamem — an Iron Age scribal interpretatio in stone. Preserves the heavenly storm-lord; the Phoenician god lacks Tarhunz's grape-and-grain cult.

citations.reference: Phoenician/Aramaic inscriptions; Temple of Baalshamin, Palmyra

variants.description: Philo describes drought-time prayer toward the sun, addressed as Beelsamen, lord of heaven, and glosses the name as Zeus.

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos, quoted in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 1.10.7

relations.subject: phoenician_chousor

relations.notes: The same craftsman god a thousand years later and in a Greek transcription: Kothar builds Baal's palace and makes Aqhat's bow at Ugarit; Chousor invents iron in Philo.

sources.claim: Chousor is the craftsman figure of Philo of Byblos's Phoenician History, credited with the invention of iron and metalwork, and identified as the Phoenician form of the Ugaritic Kothar-wa-Hasis.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Chousor and his relation to Kothar-wa-Khasis.

Trilingual inscription equating Eshmun with Asclepius

sources.reference: Hdt. 2.43-44 (Herodotus visits both the Tyrian Heracles temple and the Egyptian Heracles to investigate the equation; concludes the Phoenician Melqart cult is the older); Diod. 5.20; Sil. Italicus 3.21

citations.reference: Tyrian inscriptions; Josephus, Antiquities (egersis of Herakles)
E. Lipiński, on the etymology milk-qart

names.value: 'Uprightness', 'level dealing' — from a root meaning straight or level. The word-pair sedeq-mishor is standing Northwest Semitic idiom for justice.

relations.subject: phoenician_misor

sources.reference: Reference treatment pairing Misor with Sydyk.

relations.notes: The other half of the word-pair.

relations.subject: phoenician_misor

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos: 'From Misor came Taautos, who discovered how to write the first letters.'

relations.notes: Father of the inventor of the alphabet, which makes writing the child of uprightness — a genealogy that is clearly doing moral work as well as narrative work.

sources.claim: Misor is a personification of uprightness in Philo of Byblos's Phoenician History, paired with Sydyk and named as the father of Taautos, the inventor of letters.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Sydyk and Misor.

relations.subject: phoenician_resheph
relations.notes: Reciprocal of canaanite_resheph.equated-with — Ugaritic Rašpu and Phoenician-Cypriot Reshep are one plague-archer god in successive streams. Preserves arrows, fever, and gatekeeping of the sun; the Cypriot cult adds the Apollo identification.

relations.subject: phoenician_resheph

sources.reference: Phoenician-Cypriot bilingual dedications from Idalion, Cyprus (Reshep Mikal = Apollo Amyklos), 4th c. BCE

relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_hesiod_apollo.interpretatio — Cypriot bilinguals equate Reshep with Apollo. Preserves the plague-archer whose arrows bring fever — Apollo's Iliad 1 aspect exactly; breaks on Apollo's oracular, musical, and ephebic sides.

citations.reference: Phoenician inscriptions (Resheph of the Garden, lord of the arrow)

names.value: 'Righteousness' or 'justice' — the same root as the Hebrew tsedeq, and the element in the name Melchizedek, 'my king is Sydyk' or 'the king is righteousness'.

relations.subject: phoenician_sydyk

sources.reference: Reference treatment pairing Sydyk and Misor as the personifications of Justice and Righteousness in Philo's account.

relations.notes: Always paired with Misor. The two words are near-synonyms in Semitic and the pair is a hendiadys — 'justice and uprightness' — that Philo has made into two people.

sources.claim: Sydyk is a personification of justice in Philo of Byblos's Phoenician History, paired with Misor, and the element behind the name Melchizedek.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Sydyk and Misor as Phoenician personifications of ideals.

names.value: The Egyptian Thoth, rendered through Phoenician into Greek; Philo says explicitly that this is the god the Egyptians call Thouth, the Alexandrians Thoth and the Greeks Hermes.

relations.subject: phoenician_taautos

sources.reference: Philo of Byblos, identifying Taautos with the god the Egyptians call Thouth.

relations.notes: Philo says the identification outright, which makes this one of the few cross-tradition equations in the registry that comes from an ancient source rather than a modern comparison.

sources.claim: Taautos is the inventor of letters in Philo of Byblos's Phoenician History, son of Misor, whom Philo identifies with the Egyptian Thoth and the Greek Hermes.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Philo of Byblos, who claims to draw on a Phoenician source by Sanchuniathon, who in turn drew on the teachings of Taautos.

relations.subject: phoenician_tanit

citations.reference: Carthaginian votive inscriptions to 'rbt tnt pn bʿl'

relations.subject: sarmatian_great_goddess

sources.reference: Y. Ustinova, The Supreme Gods of the Bosporan Kingdom (1999)

relations.notes: Scholarly continuity-identification of the Sarmatian enthroned great goddess with Scythian Argimpasa. No native Sarmatian theonym survives, so the equation rests on iconographic continuity alone.

sources.claim: The Scythian Great Goddess (Argimpasa/Artimpasa, the snake-legged ancestress) had no recorded distinct Sarmatian name, but her type as winged fertility-goddess, mistress of beasts and patroness of sovereignty and divination persisted into Sarmatian religion and survived at the Bosporus as the Celestial Aphrodite/Apatouros.

citations.reference: Y. Ustinova, The Supreme Gods of the Bosporan Kingdom (Brill, 1999)

sources.claim: The prominence of armed priestess- and warrior-women in Sarmatian burials is connected by scholars to the continuing cult of a sovereign female deity of the Scytho-Sarmatian Iranian world.

citations.reference: V.I. Guliaev, 'The Cult of Female Warriors and Rulers in the Scythian and Sarmatian Cultures' (2019)

relations.subject: sarmatian_sword_god

sources.reference: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.2.23 (the Alans worship a bare sword as Mars)

relations.notes: Ammianus: a sword fixed in the earth is worshipped 'as Mars'. Preserves war-divinity in aniconic steppe form; breaks on everything civic and calendrical in Roman Mars, including his agrarian roots.

relations.subject: sarmatian_sword_god
relations.notes: Standard scholarly identification of the Sarmatian/Alanic sword-cult as the continuation of the Scythian akinakes-cult Herodotus describes. Same aniconic sword-worship; six centuries separate the attestations.

sources.claim: The Alani (a Sarmatian people) have no temples or shrines but fix a bared sword in the earth and worship it as Mars, the war-god of their territories.
This Alanic sword-cult is the late continuation of the Scythian worship of 'Ares' as a planted iron sword (Hdt 4.62); the rite is read as the erection of an axis mundi joining men and gods.

citations.reference: 'Sarmatian Religion,' Encyclopedia of Religion (M. Eliade, ed.); D.S. Raevskiy (1977)

relations.subject: scythian_agathyrsos

relations.subject: scythian_agathyrsos
relations.notes: Eldest brother of Scythes, the youngest, who alone strung their father's bow and stayed to rule.

sources.claim: Eldest son of Heracles and the viper-maiden; unable to bend the bow, he is sent out of the land and becomes eponym of the Agathyrsi.

relations.subject: scythian_anacharsis

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.76 (Anacharsis of the royal Scythian house; uncle of King Idanthyrsus)

relations.notes: Sage of the royal Scythian house (son of Gnurus); the royal Scythians (Paralatae) descend from the first king Kolaxais, recorded as lineage descent parallel to King Idanthyrsus.

sources.claim: Anacharsis, a Scythian of the royal line who travelled widely among the Greeks, was killed by the Scythian king Saulios for adopting the Greek rites of the Mother of the Gods (Cybele) at Kyzikos; the Scythians shun foreign customs.
He became a Greek byword for the wise 'noble savage' and was later counted among the Seven Sages by some traditions.

citations.reference: Diogenes Laertius 1.101-105; J.F. Kindstrand, Anacharsis: The Legend and the Apophthegmata (1981)

relations.subject: scythian_api
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_papaios.spouse — Herodotos glosses Api as Earth and reports the Scythians hold Earth to be the wife of Zeus (Papaios): the sky-father/earth-mother pair.

relations.subject: scythian_api
relations.notes: Hdt: 'Earth (Ge), in Scythian Api', wife of Papaios. Preserves the sky-earth primal pair; breaks on Api's likely water-element (the name suggests Iranian ap- 'water'), which Hdt's gloss flattens.

sources.claim: Herodotos identifies Api with Earth (Ge/Gaia) and pairs her with Zeus-Papaios in the second rank of Scythian gods.

Although Herodotos glosses her only as Earth, her name continues Iranian āp- 'water', so she is read as an earth-and-water mother-goddess, consort of the sky-father; some scholars connect the Scythian Snake-Legged ancestress to her as her daughter.

citations.reference: V.I. Abaev (1949); R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'; S.S. Bessonova, Religioznye predstavleniya skifov (1983)

relations.subject: scythian_ares
relations.notes: Reciprocal of sarmatian_sword_god.equated-with — Standard scholarly identification of the Sarmatian/Alanic sword-cult as the continuation of the Scythian akinakes-cult Herodotus describes. Same aniconic sword-worship; six centuries separate the attestations.

relations.subject: scythian_ares
relations.notes: Hdt names only 'Ares' for the sword-god — no Scythian theonym survives. Preserves pure war-divinity; breaks on cult form: the akinakes on a brush-platform altar with captive sacrifice has no Greek analogue.

sources.claim: Scythian religion was largely aniconic, raising neither images nor altars except to Ares; to Ares each district sets up an iron scimitar on a brushwood pile as his image and offers yearly sacrifices of sheep, goats and horses, and the blood of one in a hundred war-captives.
The sword-on-the-altar war-god has no recorded native name; he is interpreted as a god of kingship, victory and the warrior function, the planted sword serving as an axis mundi joining men and gods.

citations.reference: D.S. Raevskiy (1977); R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'

relations.subject: scythian_argimpasa

sources.reference: Y. Ustinova, The Supreme Gods of the Bosporan Kingdom (1999)

relations.notes: Reciprocal of sarmatian_great_goddess.equated-with — Scholarly continuity-identification of the Sarmatian enthroned great goddess with Scythian Argimpasa. No native Sarmatian theonym survives, so the equation rests on iconographic continuity alone.

relations.subject: scythian_argimpasa
relations.notes: Hdt equates Argimpasa with Aphrodite Ourania, the celestial Venus-goddess. Preserves the great-goddess-of-love slot; breaks on Argimpasa's sovereignty and her ecstatic Enarees diviners, alien to Aphrodite.

sources.claim: Herodotos equates the Scythian goddess with Aphrodite Ourania (the Heavenly Aphrodite), worshipped by all Scythians; the transmitted Greek form is Ἀργίμπασα.
Her priests, the Enarees, suffer the 'female disease' and practise a linden-bark divination; this cult of effeminate diviners is tied to the goddess.

Recent scholarship (Ustinova) treats the original native theonym as Artimpasa (Ἀρτίμπασα), the form Argimpasa being a Greek scribal/aural corruption; she is the Scythian reflex of the Iranian goddess Arti/Aṣ̌i, an androgynous goddess of fertility, sovereignty and the priestly power, continued in the Bosporan cult of Aphrodite Apatouros/Ourania.

citations.reference: Y. Ustinova, The Supreme Gods of the Bosporan Kingdom (Brill, 1999)

relations.subject: scythian_ariapeithes
relations.notes: Skyles, the Bacchic king, was the son of Ariapeithes by an Istrian woman who taught him Greek.

relations.subject: scythian_ariapeithes
relations.notes: Octamasades, Skyles half-brother who succeeded and beheaded him, was likewise a son of Ariapeithes, by a daughter of the Thracian king Teres.

citations.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.78 (Godley): Ariapeithes king of the Scythians, father of Skyles by an Istrian woman, slain by Spargapeithes the Agathyrsian

relations.subject: scythian_arpoxais
relations.notes: Middle brother of Kolaxais in the three-sons myth of Targitaos.

relations.subject: scythian_arpoxais
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_lipoxais.sibling — Eldest and middle of the three sons of Targitaos; both repelled by the blazing sky-fallen gold.

sources.claim: Middle son of Targitaos; ancestor of the tribes called Catiari and Traspians.

Some scholars read the first element as Iranian *ap- 'water', aligning the middle brother with the second (warrior) function and/or the waters in trifunctional and tripartite-cosmos analyses of the myth.

citations.reference: G. Dumezil, Romans de Scythie et d'alentour (1978); D.S. Raevskiy, Ocherki ideologii skifo-sakskikh plemen (1977)

relations.subject: scythian_borysthenis
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_papaios.lover — In the Scythians' own origin myth, Targitaos is born of Zeus (Papaios) and a daughter of the river Borysthenes.

sources.claim: The mother of the first man Targitaos is a daughter of the river Borysthenes (the Dnieper), joined with Zeus-Papaios.
She represents the deified Dnieper, the river the Scythians revered most after the Istros (Hdt 4.53); a water-nymph consort of the sky-god in the dynastic charter.

citations.reference: D.S. Raevskiy (1977); R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'

relations.subject: scythian_gelonos
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_agathyrsos.sibling — Elder brothers in the Pontic-Greek variant: sons of Heracles and the serpent-legged maiden, both failed the bow-and-girdle test and were sent away.

relations.subject: scythian_gelonos
relations.notes: Middle brother of Scythes in the Heraclean variant of the origin myth.

sources.claim: Middle son of Heracles and the viper-maiden; also failing the bow-test, he is driven out and becomes eponym of the Geloni.

relations.subject: scythian_gnurus
relations.notes: Anacharsis the sage is named son of Gnurus in the royal Scythian pedigree.

relations.subject: scythian_gnurus
relations.notes: King Saulios, brother of Anacharsis, is likewise a son of Gnurus.

citations.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.76 (Godley): Anacharsis son of Gnurus; Gnurus son of Lykos, of the royal Scythian house

relations.subject: scythian_goitosyros
relations.notes: Hdt: 'Apollo, in Scythian Goitosyros.' The match runs through solar brightness; nothing oracular, musical, or archer-like is attested for the Scythian god — the equation is Herodotus's grid, not cult.

sources.claim: Herodotos equates the Scythian Goitosyros (Oetosyrus) with Apollo, placing him in the third rank of gods worshipped by all Scythians.

The name is analysed as *Gaiθā-sūra, from Iranian gaiθā- 'herds, possessions' (cf. Avestan gaēθā-) + sūra- 'strong, mighty' (cf. Avestan sūra-), i.e. 'mighty in flocks'. Because Apollo was a solar god in Greek thought, Goitosyros is taken as the Scythian sun-god; his function has also been compared with Iranian Mithra and Vayu.

citations.reference: V.I. Abaev (1949); R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'

relations.subject: scythian_herakles
relations.notes: The serpent-legged mistress of Hylaea withheld his strayed mares until he lay with her; from the union came Agathyrsus, Gelonus and Scythes.

relations.subject: scythian_herakles
relations.notes: Pontic Greeks told the Scythian genealogy with Heracles fathering Scythes on the snake-legged maiden; Hdt also lists 'Heracles' among Scythian gods. Preserves the strongman-forefather; the native name is lost.

sources.claim: In the version told by the Pontic Greeks, Heracles, driving Geryon's cattle, mates with a viper-maiden (half-woman, half-snake) in the land of Hylaia; she bears three sons, Agathyrsus, Gelonus and Scythes, and Heracles leaves a bow and a clasped belt to test which son shall rule.
This Heracles is generally understood by modern scholars as the Greek interpretatio of the native forefather Targitaos.

citations.reference: G. Dumezil (1978); A. Ivantchik, 'The Scythian rule over Asia' and related studies; R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica

relations.subject: scythian_idanthyrsos
relations.notes: In his defiance of Darius, Idanthyrsos names as his only masters 'Zeus my ancestor' (Papaios) and Hestia queen of the Scythians.

relations.subject: scythian_idanthyrsos
relations.notes: The Royal Scythian kings (Paralatae) descend from Kolaxais, youngest son of Targitaos; Idanthyrsos is king of the Royal Scythians.

sources.claim: Idanthyrsos was the king of the (Royal) Scythians who led the mobile resistance to Darius I's invasion and, in his message, named only Papaios-Zeus his forefather and Tabiti-Hestia, 'queen of the Scythians', as his lords.

relations.subject: scythian_kolaxais
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_arpoxais.sibling — Middle brother of Kolaxais in the three-sons myth of Targitaos.

relations.subject: scythian_kolaxais
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_lipoxais.sibling — Eldest brother of the youngest, Kolaxais, who alone could take up the burning gold and so received the kingship.

sources.claim: Youngest son of Targitaos; only he could take the four golden objects that fell blazing from heaven (plough-with-yoke, battle-axe, cup), so the brothers gave him sole kingship; ancestor of the royal tribe, the Paralatae.

The name's second element is Old Iranian *xšaya 'ruling'; the first element is widely connected to a sun-word (*huar-/*hvarya-), giving 'Sun-King', the divinely solar sovereign of the royal Scythians.

citations.reference: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians' (R. Schmitt et al.); B. Lincoln, Nordlit 33 (2014)

relations.subject: scythian_lipoxais
relations.notes: Eldest and middle of the three sons of Targitaos; both repelled by the blazing sky-fallen gold.

relations.subject: scythian_lipoxais
relations.notes: Eldest brother of the youngest, Kolaxais, who alone could take up the burning gold and so received the kingship.

sources.claim: Eldest of Targitaos' three sons; ancestor of the Scythian tribe called Auchatae.

His name (like his brothers') ends in the Old Iranian element *xšaya 'ruling, reign'; in Dumezil's trifunctional reading the eldest brother and his line correspond to the lowest (third) productive function.

citations.reference: G. Dumezil, Romans de Scythie et d'alentour (1978); B. Lincoln, Nordlit 33 (2014)

names.value: Iranian personal name, second element cf. Thagimasadas / *mazda-

relations.subject: scythian_octamasades
relations.notes: Brothers, both sons of Ariapeithes; the Scythians deposed the philhellene Skyles in favour of Octamasades.

relations.subject: scythian_octamasades
relations.notes: Octamasades pursued, took and beheaded his fugitive brother Skyles after the prisoner-exchange with Sitalces.

citations.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.80 (Godley): the Scythians set up Octamasades, brother of Skyles, as king; he received Skyles in exchange and beheaded him

relations.subject: scythian_papaios
relations.notes: Herodotos glosses Api as Earth and reports the Scythians hold Earth to be the wife of Zeus (Papaios): the sky-father/earth-mother pair.

relations.subject: scythian_papaios
relations.notes: In the Scythians' own origin myth, Targitaos is born of Zeus (Papaios) and a daughter of the river Borysthenes.

relations.subject: scythian_papaios
relations.notes: Hdt: 'Zeus, in Scythian most rightly named Papaios' ('father'). Preserves the sky-father paired with Earth; breaks on the absence of any Scythian sovereignty-myth or thunder-weapon for Papaios.

sources.claim: Herodotos equates Papaios with Zeus and ranks him (with Api) just below Tabiti; he comments that the name Papaios is 'most rightly' given to Zeus.
Papaios is the divine father of the first man Targitaos in the Scythian genealogical myth.

The name reflects Scythian *Pāpaya 'Father', a hypocoristic/reduplicated kinship word; he is the sky-father, consort of the earth-goddess Api, and is sometimes read against Iranian sovereign sky-gods.

citations.reference: V.I. Abaev (1949); R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'

relations.subject: scythian_saulios
relations.notes: Saulios and Anacharsis are brothers, sons of Gnurus; Saulios shot Anacharsis dead for adopting Greek rites.

relations.subject: scythian_saulios
relations.notes: Anacharsis is named the uncle of King Idanthyrsus; Idanthyrsus is therefore son of Saulios, Anacharsis brother.

relations.subject: scythian_saulios
relations.notes: As the killer of his brother, Saulios is also Anacharsis slayer; the kinship is fratricidal.

citations.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.76 (Godley): Saulios the king, brother of Anacharsis, killed him; he was father of Idanthyrsus, whose uncle Anacharsis was

relations.subject: scythian_skyles

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.78-80 (Skyles, son of King Ariapeithes)

relations.notes: Bacchic king of the royal Scythians; as a royal Scythian he descends from the first king Kolaxais, recorded as lineage descent parallel to King Idanthyrsus.

sources.claim: Skyles, a Scythian king with a Greek (Istrian) mother, secretly took up Greek ways at Olbia/Borysthenes and had himself initiated into the rites of the Bacchic Dionysos; exposed reveling with the god, he was overthrown and beheaded by his brother Octamasades.
Herodotos pairs his fate with that of Anacharsis to show that the Scythians sternly refuse foreign religious customs; his story is read as a tragedy of cultural boundary-crossing.

citations.reference: G. Hinge, 'Dionysos and Herakles in Scythia,' Black Sea Studies 8 (2008); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'

relations.subject: scythian_skythes
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_agathyrsos.sibling — Eldest brother of Scythes, the youngest, who alone strung their father's bow and stayed to rule.

relations.subject: scythian_skythes
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_gelonos.sibling — Middle brother of Scythes in the Heraclean variant of the origin myth.

sources.claim: Scythes, youngest son of Heracles and the viper-maiden, is the only one able to bend his father's bow and wear the belt; he becomes king and eponymous ancestor of the Scythians.

relations.subject: scythian_snake_legged_goddess
relations.notes: Reciprocal of scythian_herakles.lover — The serpent-legged mistress of Hylaea withheld his strayed mares until he lay with her; from the union came Agathyrsus, Gelonus and Scythes.

sources.claim: In the Pontic-Greek myth the mother of the Scythian kings is a mixoparthenos, woman above and serpent below, mistress of the land of Hylaia, who keeps Heracles' horses until he fathers three sons on her.

She corresponds to the widely-attested Scythian anguipede 'Snake-Legged Goddess' of Black-Sea art, a chthonic life-giving ancestress read as a daughter of Api and closely (but not wholly) identified with Argimpasa/Artimpasa; the Greeks assimilated her to Hecate near the Borysthenes.

citations.reference: Y. Ustinova, The Supreme Gods of the Bosporan Kingdom (1999); S.S. Bessonova, Religioznye predstavleniya skifov (1983)

relations.subject: scythian_tabiti
relations.notes: Hdt: 'Hestia, in Scythian Tabiti', whom they honor most of all. Preserves the hearth-fire's primacy; breaks on rank — Tabiti is the supreme royal sovereign, far above marginal Olympian Hestia.

sources.claim: Tabiti is the deity the Scythians honour above all; Herodotos equates her with Hestia and reports she was revered most of all the gods.
King Idanthyrsos names her 'mistress (queen) of the Scythians' in his message to Darius, marking her as a sovereign hearth-goddess bound to the royal house.

The Hellenised Ταβιτί continues Scythian *Tapatī 'the Burning One', from the Indo-Iranian root *tap- 'to be hot, burn' (Avestan tāpaiieⁱti, Vedic verb tapati; cf. the Vedic solar-goddess Tapatī). She is read as a fire- and hearth-sovereign of the first (sacral) function.

citations.reference: V.I. Abaev, Istoriko-etimologicheskii slovar' osetinskogo yazyka; R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'

sources.claim: Targitaos is the first man in the Scythian self-account, son of Zeus (Papaios) and a daughter of the river Borysthenes.

Older derivation read the name as *Darga-tavah 'whose might is far-reaching'; this is now judged untenable because Old Iranian /d/ had shifted to /δ/ (then /l/) in Scythian, and the form is re-analysed as Targī̆tavah 'possessing the strength of (the goddess) Tarkā'. He is widely equated with the Pontic-Greek Heracles of the parallel myth.

citations.reference: V.I. Abaev, Osetinskii yazyk i fol'klor (1949); R. Schmitt & contributors, 'Scythians,' Encyclopaedia Iranica

relations.subject: scythian_thagimasadas
relations.notes: Hdt: 'Poseidon, in Scythian Thagimasadas', worshipped only by the Royal Scythians. Preserves the water-and-horse pairing — the strongest functional fit in his list; breaks on sea and earthquake.

sources.claim: Herodotos says that the Royal Scythians alone, beyond the gods worshipped by all, sacrifice to Poseidon, whom they call Thagimasadas.

Identified with Poseidon as a god of waters and horse-taming; the Royal Scythians' exclusive worship and his role as an ancestral figure parallel Poseidon-Erechtheus at Athens. The second element of the name has been linked to Iranian *mazdā-.

citations.reference: R. Schmitt et al., Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Scythians'; Y. Ustinova (1999)

sources.claim: Eryx is the eponymous hero of Mount Eryx and its city in western Sicily, a king celebrated for his strength as a fighter and named as a son of the goddess of love; the mountain carried an Elymian sanctuary of a mother goddess long before Greek or Roman contact.

citations.reference: Reference treatment of Eryx, king of Sicily and son of Aphrodite.
Reference treatment of the Elymian sanctuary on Mount Eryx, venerating a mother goddess of fertility and the heavens.

variants.claim: Eryx's father is given differently in different accounts.
variants.description: His mother is consistently the goddess of love; his father is variously Butes the Argonaut and Poseidon. Because the accounts disagree, only the maternal line is authored, and the record's tier follows from that single divine parent.

sources.reference: Reference treatment of Eryx noting the divergent paternities.

relations.subject: thracian_bendis
relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_hesiod_artemis.interpretatio — Hdt names Artemis among Thrace's three gods; lexicographers gloss Bendis as Thracian Artemis. Preserves the huntress with spears; Athens nonetheless gave Bendis her own Bendideia, not Artemis's cult.

sources.claim: Bendis is a Thracian huntress-and-moon goddess given an official Athenian cult, with a sanctuary at the Piraeus and the state festival Bendideia (first held 429 BCE), famous for its nighttime mounted torch-race.
Her name is generally derived from PIE *bhendh- 'to bind', suggesting an original function over marital/communal bonds before her hunt-and-moon profile dominated in Greek reception.

citations.reference: Standard etymological treatments of Bendis (< *bhendh- 'bind'), e.g. summarized in Theoi.com, citing Hellenistic lexica

relations.subject: thracian_cabeiri
relations.notes: In the Argive genealogy of Acusilaus the three Kabeiroi are sons of Kamillos (Kadmilos), a variant strand beside his role as their attendant.

relations.subject: thracian_cabeiri

sources.reference: Scholia on Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.917 (citing Mnaseas)

relations.notes: Reciprocal of thracian_kadmilos.companion — Kasmilos/Kadmilos is the fourth of the Samothracian Great Gods, the Hermes-like attendant who serves the triad in the mystery cult.

sources.claim: The Kabeiroi/Great Gods of Samothrace are chthonic mystery deities whose Samothracian cult Herodotus traces to the pre-Greek Pelasgians and which ancient sources connect to Thracian (and Phrygian) origins; their numbered members were glossed as Axieros, Axiokersa, Axiokersos and Kasmilos (≈ Demeter, Persephone, Hades, Hermes).

citations.reference: Mnaseas and the scholia naming Axieros, Axiokersa, Axiokersos, Kasmilos

sources.claim: Initiation conferred protection at sea and was open to all people regardless of sex, age, class or nationality.

sources.reference: M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (Oxford 2007), ch. 4 'Sky and Earth'

relations.notes: Greek Semele, mother of Dionysus, continues Thraco-Phrygian zemelo 'earth'; in the source-stratum the ecstatic god is the earth-mother's son.

relations.subject: thracian_dionysus
relations.notes: Reciprocal of thracian_orpheus.companion — Founder of the Dionysiac mysteries; in Aeschylus' Bassarai strand the god, slighted for Helios, sends his maenads against the singer.

relations.subject: thracian_dionysus
relations.notes: Reciprocal of thracian_rhesus.companion — The mourning Muse foretells that Rhesus will lie in the silver-veined earth as an anthropodaimon, a 'prophet of Bacchus' on Pangaion.

relations.subject: thracian_dionysus

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 5.7, 7.111 (oracle of Dionysus among the Satrae)

relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_hesiod_dionysus.interpretatio — Greeks read the Thracian mountain-ecstatic as Dionysus; his Pangaion-region oracle rivals Delphi in Hdt's telling. Preserves frenzy and prophecy; the native god's fox-skin and oracle-lordship are distinct.

sources.claim: Herodotus names Dionysus (with Ares and Artemis) among the chief gods of the Thracians and describes a mountain oracle of Dionysus among the Satrae, staffed by a priestess and the Bessi interpreters.
Bassareus (from the fox-skin bassaris) and Sabos/Sabazios are Thracian names of Dionysus, and much of the Dionysiac ecstatic complex is held to be of Thracian/Thraco-Phrygian origin.

citations.reference: Walter Burkert, Greek Religion (1985), on the Thracian roots of Dionysiac ecstasy

names.value: The Thracian Horseman, Hero-God of the Reliefs

sources.claim: The Thracian Horseman (Heros) is the central hero-god of Thracian votive and funerary reliefs, attested on over 2,000 monuments, embodying chthonic, healing, hunting and protective functions and syncretized under Rome with Apollo, Asklepios, Silvanus and others.

citations.reference: The Thracian Horseman relief and inscription corpus, Thrace and the western Black Sea

sources.claim: His original Thracian name is lost; 'Heros' is the generic Greek label, and he bears many local cult-epithets (Karabazmos, Manimazos, Pyrmerula, Salenos, etc.).

citations.reference: Inscribed dedications giving epithets Karabazmos, Manimazos, Pyrmerula, Salenos

relations.subject: thracian_kabeiro

sources.reference: Scholia on Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.917; Strabo, Geography 10.3.21 (citing Acusilaus, FGrH 2 F 20)

relations.notes: In the Acusilaus genealogy Kabeiro, by Hephaistos, is the mother of Kadmilos (Kasmilos), the attendant and father of the Samothracian Kabeiroi. Kadmilos already carries her name in his record as his mother.

citations.reference: Strabo, Geography 10.3.21 (citing Acusilaus, FGrH 2 F 20); scholia on Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.917 (Kabeiro daughter of Proteus, by Hephaistos mother of Kadmilos and the Kabeiroi)

sources.claim: Kadmilos (Kasmilos/Casmilus) is the divine youthful attendant in the Samothracian mysteries, identified with Hermes and named in some traditions as father of the Kabeiroi (son of Hephaistos and the nymph Kabeiro).

citations.reference: Akusilaos and the scholia on Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.917

relations.subject: thracian_kandaon

sources.reference: Lycophron, Alexandra 938 with Tzetzes' scholia (Kandaon as Thracian Ares)

relations.notes: Lycophron's gloss-tradition renders Kandaon as the Thracian Ares. Preserves the war-god slot Hdt 5.7 gives Thrace; the native god's wolf-associations have no equivalent in the Greek Ares.

sources.claim: Kandaon/Candaon is a Thracian god identified with Ares, said to be worshipped by the Crestonian Thracians, attested through Lycophron's Alexandra and its scholia.

citations.reference: Lycophron, Alexandra, with scholia (Candaon = Ares of the Crestonians)

sources.claim: Kendrisos is a Thracian Rider-god syncretized with Apollo as the patron deity of Philippopolis (Plovdiv), with the local epithet attached to Apollo (Apollo Kendrisos/Kendreisenos) and a civic festival, the Kendreiseia Pythia.

citations.reference: Inscriptions and coins of Philippopolis (Apollo Kendrisos / Kendreiseia games)

names.value: Orpheus, the Thracian Singer and Founder of the Mysteries

relations.subject: thracian_orpheus
relations.notes: Founder of the Dionysiac mysteries; in Aeschylus' Bassarai strand the god, slighted for Helios, sends his maenads against the singer.

relations.subject: thracian_orpheus

sources.reference: M. L. West, The Orphic Poems (1983)

relations.notes: Reciprocal of greek_orpheus.equated-with — The registry's Greek Orpheus and the Thracian culture-hero are the same figure seen from two traditions; the Greeks themselves always marked him Thracian. The Thracian entry stresses the mystery-founder role.

sources.claim: Orpheus is the Thracian singer, son of the Muse Calliope and the Thracian king Oeagrus (some say Apollo), whose song moved nature and who is credited as founder of the Orphic mysteries; ancient sources treat his cult and rites as borrowed by the Greeks from his Thracian people.
His death by dismemberment at the hands of Thracian women near Mount Pangaion, where he had honored Apollo at the oracle of Dionysus, is recounted in Aeschylus' lost Bassarids and by later poets.

citations.reference: Summary of Aeschylus, Bassarids (Eratosthenes/[pseudo-Eratosthenes]); Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.1-66

relations.subject: thracian_sabazios

sources.reference: E. N. Lane, Corpus Cultus Iovis Sabazii (1983-1989)

relations.notes: The Thracian and Phrygian Sabazios are one Thraco-Phrygian god split by transmission region; the corpus of monuments treats the cult as a single continuum. Both carry the *Dyeus-derived sky-father element.

sources.claim: Sabazios is the Thraco-Phrygian sky-father and horseman god, his name's -zios element deriving from PIE *dyeus (cf. Zeus/deus); Greeks identified him with both Zeus and Dionysus, Romans chiefly with Jupiter.
His distinctive cult emblem is the votive bronze hand raised in blessing, covered with serpents and other symbols; the snake also figured in his initiation rites.

citations.reference: Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus 2.16; Firmicus Maternus, De errore 10

relations.subject: thracian_semele

sources.reference: Diodorus Siculus 3.62-64; Phrygian inscription invoking Diounsis Zemelo
M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (2007), on Zemele/Semele

relations.notes: Thraco-Phrygian earth-mother Zemele, mother of the Thracian Dionysus, who already carries the reciprocal 'descendant of' edge.

sources.claim: The name Semele is widely judged to be Thraco-Phrygian, an earth-goddess theonym (Zemelā) from a PIE root for 'earth', cognate with Baltic Žemyna/Žemelė and matching the Phrygian formula 'diōs zemelō' (Zeus and Earth).

citations.reference: Julius Pokorny, Indogermanisches etymologisches Wörterbuch (Thracian Zemele 'mother earth')

sources.claim: Burkert cautions that while Semele is 'manifestly non-Greek', a firm Thraco-Phrygian 'earth' meaning is hard to prove conclusively.

citations.reference: Walter Burkert, Greek Religion (1985), on Semele and the Dionysiac complex

sources.claim: Zibelthiurdos (Zbelsurdos) is a Thracian god of heaven, lightning and rain known mainly from Roman-period epigraphic monuments at Pautalia and Serdica, iconographically assimilated to Zeus the Thunderer with thunderbolt and eagle.

citations.reference: Roman votive inscriptions/monuments from Pautalia and Serdica

sources.claim: His name appears to contain the same Proto-Indo-European root as the Getic Gebeleizis, with a different phonetic development, supporting the reading of a Thracian sky/thunder god.

citations.reference: Comparative etymological treatments linking Zibelthiurdos and Gebeleizis to a PIE storm/sky theonym

relations.subject: zoroastrian_zurvan

sources.reference: Reference treatment: the Zurwanite credo postulated Zurwan as a third entity who generated both Ohrmazd and Ahriman.

relations.notes: The kind names the doctrine inside itself, because the claim is true only within it. Orthodox Zoroastrianism does not accept that Ahura Mazda was generated by anything, and writing a plain 'father-of' edge here would enter a sectarian position as though it were the tradition's own. Nothing is entered in anyone's parentIds for the same reason.
